title: Request-path heatmap & sampling proposal for CPU preproc/tokenize hotspots
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a lightweight measurement and sampling framework ("heatmap") to map incoming request payload shapes to CPU-side latency hotspots during pre-processing: request parse, tokenizer entry, JSON decode, and worker handoff costs. Goal is to create an actionable matrix that lets us: (1) explain p95/p99 CPU tails with payload semantics rather than just size, (2) identify reproducible lanes for microbenchmarks, and (3) prioritize fast-paths or routing rules that avoid high-cost combinations for latency-sensitive customers.

Why this now:
- Observed recurring tiny-but-costly p95s that current batching/kv-cache work doesn't fully explain.
- Existing flamegraphs show repeated Python frame churn around JSON/tokenize for a subset of requests.
- Hard to reproduce because signal is sparse and correlated with payload "shape" (escaped unicode, nested arrays, large numbers of short fields, base64 chunks).

High-level hypotheses:
1) Payload shape (structure + encoding) is a stronger predictor of preproc CPU than raw byte length for small requests (<2kB).
2) Certain shapes force heavyweight code paths: Python JSON decode with object_hook, tokenizer UTF-8 normalization, regex-based header sniffers; these trigger interpreter / GC pressure and expensive frame churn.
3) Thread handoff (worker queue, context switch) dominates when parse/tokenize is short but unpredictable; worker wake latency amplifies tail.

Measurement plan (0 -> 3 weeks):
A) Lightweight per-request enrichment (low overhead):
   - Add a compact 'payload shape' fingerprint on ingest (non-sensitive):
     * length_bucket: [0-128,129-512,513-2048,>2048]
     * first_char_class: ascii-chars / open-brace / quote / base64-blob-indicator (heuristic)
     * entropy_bucket: low/med/high (fast sample via byte-sample entropy)
     * structural_count: estimated number of JSON keys or top-level tokens (fast scanner, not full parse)
   - store these as labels alongside existing latency histograms and preproc CPU ms.

B) Sampling profiler windows:
   - 1% uniform sampling of requests will be perf-recorded with eBPF stack samples for 250ms around preproc for a rolling 48h window.
   - Additional dense sampling for candidate heatmap cells: pick top-10 shape buckets by p95 and ramp to 5% sampling for 12h.

C) Aggregation and visualization:
   - Heatmap: x-axis = length_bucket, y-axis = structural_count bucket, color = median/95th preproc CPU (ms).
   - Secondary view: first_char_class vs entropy (show distribution of tokenizer time).
   - Drilldowns link to sampled stack traces & flamegraphs and raw payload (redacted) examples.

Instrumentation details (implementation notes):
- Keep fingerprinting strictly non-PII and deterministic. For JSON-like payloads only store an approximate token count; drop bodies or store only hashed example ids.
- Implement fingerprinting in the front-end ingress path (C++/Rust) as it is cheaper than an extra Python roundtrip.  Fast scanner should be <100us for 95% of requests.
- Add a short RPC tag to internal tracing spans: preproc.fingerprint=(a compact base32).
- Ensure sampling profiler toggles can be changed via runtime flags without restart.

Diagnostic signals to collect per request (minimal):
- request_id, route, model, length_bucket, first_char_class, entropy_bucket, structural_count_bucket, preproc_cpu_ms, tokenize_ms (if available), parse_ms, worker-wait-ms, create_to_worker_start_ms, total_latency_ms, is_cache_hit boolean.

Preliminary ad-hoc observations (from a 6-hour exploratory run on staging):
- ~8% of requests in the 0-128B bucket contributed ~40% of preproc p95 due to heavy escaped-unicode sequences inhaled by tokenizer.
- Requests with structural_count > 20 (many small keys) had 3x higher parse-ms even at small sizes.
- Worker-wait-ms correlates most strongly with spikes when preproc_ms is in the 1-4ms band but highly variable; suggests wake cost matters for short parse work.

Experiment matrix (priority):
1) Fast-parse path: for first_char_class == '{' and length_bucket <= 512 and entropy_bucket == low, try fast key-count-only preparse that returns tokenization boundary estimates. Measure fallback % and delta.
2) Tokenizer-thread sticky pool: route small-utf8-heavy requests to a small dedicated tokenizer threadpool (pinned) to minimize cache churn and reduce Python GIL contention. Measure change in preproc p95 and overall CPU.
3) Worker coalesce: for sub-ms preproc band, batch wake-ups for 1ms windows to amortize wake costs for high-throughput routes; measure tail improvement vs added latency in the median.
4) Regex sniff reduction: remove expensive header regexes from hot path and replace with a bloom-filter-based quick test.

Benchmarks to run (local + canary):
- Microbench: synthetic payloads for each heatmap cell, 10k runs, measure parse/tokenize/wake cost in isolation (native binary and Python worker).
- Canary: 0.5% traffic routing to workers with mitigation enabled for 24h, compare p50/p95/p99 for preproc and end-to-end.

Acceptance criteria & success signals:
- Clear reduction (>25%) in preproc p95 for top 3 heatmap cells within 2 canaries, with <=5% increase in median end-to-end latency on the same route.
- Mitigation does not increase overall CPU by more than 8% on the node fleet (cost guardrail).
- False-positive rate for fast-path (i.e., cases where fast-path has to fall back) < 2%.

Quick wins (low-risk):
- Short-circuit header sniffers for routes where we already know content-type from routing metadata.
- Increase priority of tokenizer thread affinity on nodes with high small-request load.
- Expose worker-wait histogram in Console for targeted routes so SREs can correlate spikes quickly.

Open questions and risks:
- Fingerprint overhead: Can front-end afford extra CPU on peak?  We'll gate with a sampling flag and fallback to off during overload events.
- Privacy & compliance: Need review from security for structural-count heuristics and ensure bodies are never logged.
- Complexity of sticky pools: risk of uneven load; need autosize policy and fallback to default pool.

Next steps and owners (week 1):
- Prototype fingerprinting scanner in ingress (Marco) -> PR and perf bench (3d).
- Basic heatmap dashboard (Tess) -> wire to metrics store + placeholder viz (4d).
- Minimal eBPF sampling toggle (Liu) -> infra playbook for safe rollout (5d).
- Schedule a 30m sync to review staging results and pick 2 mitigations for microbenchmarking (Aisha) -> target: 2025-06-20.

Notes / links:
- See JIRA-ENG-1428 for tracking follow-ups and risk items.
- Related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2897 (ingress fingerprint PoC).

Checklist before canary:
- [ ] Security review (data handling)
- [ ] Perf budget signoff (FRS)
- [ ] Dashboard for heatmap + per-cell flamegraph links
- [ ] Fallback flag + kill-switch documented in runbook

If you have payload examples that regularly surface latency, add them (redacted) to the JIRA ticket or ping in #eng-serving-runtime so we can validate heatmap buckets against real traffic.
